newsitem.title: UK: Melancholy engulfs metals markets, prices ailing.
newsitem.headline: Melancholy engulfs metals markets, prices ailing.

text.p: A cloud hangs over the global metals trade ahead of the industry's annual jamboree next week, with markets chastened by the biggest financial scandal in history, fragile demand and faltering prices.
World economic growth, and therefore metals demand, has been languid this year, a far cry from the upbeat outlook a year ago.
"Last year we were really looking at great stuff. This year it's been very disappointing," said Ted Arnold, metals analyst at broker Merrill Lynch.
Metals producers, traders and consumers meet in London next week for the biggest annual trade get-together.

But one metals trader will almost certainly be missing from the festivities -- former star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka who rocked world markets in June when Japan's Sumitomo Corporation uncovered a web of rogue deals.
Metals prices collapsed, traders piled up losses and regulators probed the secretive world of metals trading, which Hamanaka is said to have manipulated for over a decade.
The scandal has cost 300-year-old Sumitomo $2.6 billion.
Unassuming Hamanaka, 48, a Jekyll-and-Hyde figure who commuted from a modest suburban house, became a powerhouse in the metals world, controlling five percent of world copper supplies.
But as Sumitomo liquidated the unauthorised positions, the copper market was exposed to the raw forces of supply and demand after years of artificial buoyancy.
In the autumn of 1995, prices of the flagship industrial metal had just seen $3,000 per tonne, barely off the January peak when values hit their highest levels in nearly six years.
This week prices have been bumping around $1,900 amid a rash of slashed price forecasts by analysts.
"We're paying the price for the excesses of 1994 and early 1995," said Jim Lennon, metals analyst for Macquarie Equities.
"At that stage there was the feeling the demand was genuine, but the more and more we look, it appears that there was this mass of speculation."
Panicked consumers, fearful of more price spikes, scrambled to stock up on metals on the London Metal Exchange.

"Protracted weakness in much of Europe, coupled with signs of a stuttering in Japan and the latest mediocre data in the U.S. is persuading many end-users that the demand for their goods may simply not be there," said broker GNI in a report.
New production from a raft of new copper mines is also expected to swamp the market and put it into surplus next year.
"Even if the economies start going gangbusters let's say by the middle of next year, the point is the supply side will probably have overtaken the metals anyway," Arnold said.
Macquarie this week cut its aluminium price forecasts by 2.5 percent for 1996 and 12 percent for 1997. Aluminium touched its lowest in 2-1/4 years this week on fear of new Russian supplies.
Many dealing firms and investment banks have scaled back activities after suffering losses following the Sumitomo affair.

"A lot of people are licking their wounds. There's a lot of regrouping and you'll see a bit more downsizing over the next few years. There's nobody writing blank cheques anymore," one senior dealer said.
The industry is also jittery about ongoing investigations by regulators in Britain, Japan and the United States.
Sumitomo, sifting through a mountain of paperwork, has asked Japanese prosecutors to press charges against Hamanaka. Fraud investigators in Britain have raided several premises.

The LME itself is under a shadow as Britain's top regulator undergoes a sweeping review of the open-outcry exchange, permeated by an old world ethos more accustomed to gentlemanly handshakes than written regulations.
